title: The phone on the table
hook: a study found a phone's mere presence reduced working memory, though later studies are mixed (Ward et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the attentional blink: right after catching one thing, the mind can miss the next, and retreat meditators blinked less by grabbing less. Your line was fewer blinks. What small signal did you catch? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

Dinner with a friend. Two plates, two glasses, and a phone lying face down by the bread, silent. Nobody touches it the whole meal. It doesn't buzz once. So it isn't doing anything, right? It's just sitting there. A team of researchers wondered whether that was true. Not a phone that rings or lights up. A phone that does nothing at all, except be there. Today's word is that quiet object, and what it might cost.
screen: `FACE DOWN BY THE BREAD.` → `IT NEVER BUZZES.` → `IS IT DOING NOTHING?`

segments.voice: Adrian Ward and his colleagues asked people to do demanding mental tasks, the kind that use working memory, the mind's small scratchpad for holding things while you think. Some people left their phones face down on the desk, silenced. Some put them in a pocket or a bag. Some left them in another room. The people whose phones were in another room did best. The ones with the phone on the desk did worst. And here's the strange part: people said the phone wasn't on their mind. The researchers' idea was that some attention goes into not checking it, a quiet, steady effort to ignore something that matters to us, and that effort uses up some of the same limited capacity we've been learning about these past days. They called their paper Brain Drain. Now the honest part, and it matters. Later studies have been mixed. Some found a similar effect. Others tried and didn't find it. So this is not settled science, and anyone who says a phone on the table definitely makes you less smart is saying more than the evidence does. But look at what the idea asks us to notice. Attention is limited. Wandering costs. Holding on to the first thing makes us miss the next. A phone on the table, even silent, may be one more pull on that limited supply. And the fix the study points to costs nothing. Not willpower. Not a new app. Just distance. Another room.
screen: `FACE DOWN, POCKET, OR ANOTHER ROOM.` · `ANOTHER ROOM DID BEST.` · `LATER STUDIES ARE MIXED.` · `THE FIX IS DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put the phone in another room. If you're listening on your phone, finish this lesson first, then do it right after the bell. If not, go now: carry it out of the room, set it down, and come back. Sit, and breathe. Notice whether some part of you is still listening for it. Notice whether anything in the room gets a little quieter, or doesn't. Just watch. The bell holds the time.
The phone on the table. The idea, from one study with mixed follow-ups, that a silent phone in view may quietly draw on attention. Today's word.
screen: `THE PHONE ON THE TABLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: another room. Today, for one meal or one conversation, leave your phone in another room, and see what you notice. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Researchers test the mere-presence effect by placing participants' phones on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room, then comparing scores on working memory tasks; results across later studies have been mixed.

fork.setup: you're about to do a hard mental task, and your phone is silenced. in Ward and colleagues' study, where did people do best?
options: phone face down on the desk.
phone in a pocket or bag.
fork.reveal: another room. the ones with the phone on the desk did worst, even though it never buzzed. later studies are mixed, so it's a lead, not a law.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silent phone face down isn't doing anything.
what it means: one study found that its mere presence may draw on attention, perhaps through the effort of not checking it. later studies are mixed.
what a scholar hears: Ward and colleagues' Brain Drain study, its proposed cost of suppressing attention to a valued object, and the replication attempts that found the effect smaller or absent.

'People said the phone wasn''t on their mind' paraphrases that self-report; confirm.
Replication picture: confirm at least one replication citation (e.g. Ruiz Pardo and Minda 2022; Hartmann et al. 2020) and that 'some found a similar effect, others didn't' is fair.
